title: What a Future actually is
objectives: Explain what `poll` returns and who calls it
Predict when the body of an `async fn` starts running

sources.title: Asynchronous Programming in Rust: The Future Trait
sources.quote: The Future trait is at the center of asynchronous programming in Rust. A Future is an asynchronous computation that can produce a value

sources.title: std::future::Future
sources.quote: Futures alone are inert; they must be actively polled for the underlying computation to make progress

questions.q: A value is moved into a closure. Can the caller still use it afterwards?

options.text: No, ownership moved into the closure
options.why: A `move` transfers ownership; the caller's binding is no longer valid.
Closures borrow by default, but `move` (or a by-value use) takes ownership.

blocks.md:
If you come from JavaScript, you already know `async` and `await`. The Rust versions look the same but behave differently in one important way: a Rust future does **nothing** until something asks it to make progress [s2].

A future is a value that represents a computation which will eventually produce a result [s1]. The only thing you can do with it is call `poll`. Each call either finishes the work and returns `Poll::Ready(value)`, or does as much as it can and returns `Poll::Pending`.

Who calls `poll`? Not you. An **executor** such as Tokio calls it. Your code builds futures and hands them to the executor, and the executor decides when each one runs.

blocks.caption: The trait, simplified. The real signature uses Pin<&mut Self>.

blocks.title: "Calling an async fn starts it"
blocks.md: In JavaScript, calling an async function runs its body up to the first `await` straight away. In Rust, calling an `async fn` only **builds** a future. None of the body runs until the future is polled [s2].

steps.label: Build
steps.md: `let f = fetch_user(42);` creates a future. No network call has happened yet.

steps.label: Hand off
steps.md: `tokio::spawn(f)` gives the future to the executor.

steps.label: First poll
steps.md: The executor calls `poll`. The socket is not ready, so the future registers a waker and returns `Pending`.

steps.label: Wake
steps.md: Data arrives. The waker tells the executor this future can make progress.

steps.label: Second poll
steps.md: The executor polls again. The future finishes and returns `Ready(user)`.

blocks.answer: Only `done`. `hello()` built a future, but nothing ever polled it, so its body never ran. The compiler even warns that futures do nothing unless awaited.

blocks.title: Why the order of output surprises people
blocks.setup: Two futures are created, then awaited in the opposite order. Which message prints first?

steps.md: Create both futures. Neither body has run.
steps.code:
let a = say("a");
let b = say("b");

steps.md: Await `b` first. Awaiting polls it to completion, so `b` prints now.
Await `a` second. Only now does `a` run and print.

blocks.takeaway: Output order follows the order of **polling**, not the order of creation.

questions.q: An async fn is called but its result is never awaited or spawned. What happens?

options.why: That is JavaScript's behaviour. Rust has no implicit background executor.

options.text: It runs up to the first .await
options.why: Also JavaScript's model. In Rust even the code before the first await waits for a poll.

questions.q: What does poll return when the work cannot finish yet?

options.why: Pending means: call me again after the waker fires.
Blocking would freeze the executor thread; futures return instead.

blocks.prompt: Change the `main` from the predict step so that `hello` prints. Use Tokio.
hints: You need an executor, and `main` itself must become async.
blocks.solution: Mark `main` with `#[tokio::main]`, make it `async`, and `.await` the future.
